title: Turn a meeting transcript into minutes with AI, then verify every decision and action item
summary: Use an AI chat assistant to turn a meeting transcript into structured minutes, then verify every decision, owner, deadline, and action item against the transcript. A small synthetic example and Python script show how to make that review repeatable.
seo_title: AI Meeting Minutes Check: Verify Decisions and Actions
seo_desc: Turn a meeting transcript into minutes with AI, then verify every decision, action item, owner, and deadline against the original transcript.
audience: People who use an AI chat assistant to summarize meetings and need to confirm that the resulting minutes accurately reflect the transcript.
prerequisites: A meeting transcript saved as plain text

sections.heading: Why AI-generated meeting minutes need verification

blocks.text: An AI chat assistant can convert a long transcript into concise minutes, but concise summaries can hide errors. A tentative suggestion may become a final decision, an owner may be assigned to the wrong person, or a deadline may be inferred even though nobody stated one. For meeting records, these changes matter because people may later use the minutes to decide who must do what and by when.

The example below is synthetic. The safest workflow is to let the AI organize the transcript, then treat every decision and action item as a claim that must be traced back to specific wording in the original transcript.

blocks.title: Minutes are a derived record
blocks.text: Do not treat an AI summary as stronger evidence than the transcript. If the transcript does not clearly support a decision, owner, deadline, or commitment, the minutes should not present it as confirmed.

sections.heading: Start with a small synthetic transcript

blocks.text: Assume a fictional project team discussed a test report. The transcript contains the following statements:

rows: Mina
Let's use the revised template for the October report.
Leo
Agreed. I'll update the template and send it by October 6.
Sara
I can review the figures after Leo sends it.
Mina
Good. We should decide next week whether to add the appendix.
Leo
The supplier data may arrive on October 8, but that is not confirmed.

blocks.text: From these lines, one decision is clearly supported: the team will use the revised template for the October report. One action item is also explicit: Leo will update the template and send it by October 6. Sara intends to review the figures after Leo sends the template, but no calendar deadline is stated for Sara. The appendix is not yet approved, and October 8 is only an unconfirmed possible arrival date for supplier data.

sections.heading: Ask the AI to separate decisions from action items

blocks.text: When asking the AI to create minutes, require it to distinguish confirmed statements from unresolved points. This reduces the chance that a suggestion or estimate will be rewritten as a decision.

blocks.title: Example request to the AI
blocks.text: Turn this transcript into concise meeting minutes. Create separate sections for confirmed decisions, action items, and unresolved items. For each action item, include an owner and deadline only if the transcript states them. Do not invent deadlines or convert tentative statements into confirmed decisions. If a detail is unclear, mark it as not stated.

A reasonable AI answer might list the revised October report template as a confirmed decision; Leo — update and send the template — October 6 as an action item; Sara — review the figures after Leo sends the template — deadline not stated as another action item; and the appendix decision plus supplier data timing as unresolved items.

sections.heading: Verify each decision and action against the transcript

items: Decision: find the transcript wording that shows agreement or a final choice. A proposal such as 'we could' or 'we should decide next week' is not yet a completed decision.
Action: confirm that the transcript actually assigns or accepts a task. Do not infer a task merely because someone discussed a topic.
Owner: verify the person who accepted or was assigned the task. Similar names and pronouns can cause incorrect attribution.
Deadline: include a date only when the transcript states one clearly for that action. Do not reuse nearby dates from unrelated topics.
Dependencies: preserve wording such as 'after Leo sends it' when sequencing matters, even if no fixed date is available.
Uncertainty: keep terms such as may, possibly, not confirmed, or to be decided when the transcript uses them.

rows: Use the revised template for the October report.
Supported as a decision.
Leo will update and send the template by October 6.
Supported as an action, owner, and deadline.
Sara will review the figures by October 8.
Not supported. Sara accepted the review, but October 8 refers to possible supplier data arrival.
The appendix will be added.
Not supported. The transcript says the team will decide next week.
Supplier data will arrive on October 8.
Not supported as certain. The transcript says it may arrive then and is not confirmed.

sections.heading: Use Python to flag unsupported action details

blocks.text: The following standard-library script uses a small structured file of expected claims from the synthetic example. It checks whether supporting phrases appear in transcript.txt and writes a report to outputs/minutes_check_report.txt. It does not prove that the minutes are correct, but it can force reviewers to identify transcript evidence for each important item.

Save the transcript as transcript.txt, save the script as minutes_check.py, and run python minutes_check.py. The phrases in the script are intentionally specific to this synthetic example. For a real meeting, create a check list from the proposed minutes and link each important claim to the transcript evidence that supports it.

items: Turning 'we should decide next week' into a completed decision.
Assigning an action to the person who discussed it rather than the person who accepted it.
Adding a deadline because a nearby date appears elsewhere in the transcript.
Dropping qualifiers such as may, possibly, tentative, or not confirmed.
Combining two separate comments into a stronger statement that nobody actually made.
Treating an automatic transcript as exact even when speaker labels or words may be incorrect.

blocks.text: A transcript itself can contain transcription errors, especially with names, technical terms, numbers, or overlapping speakers. Verification against the transcript therefore checks whether the minutes match the available record; it does not prove that the transcript perfectly captured the meeting.

sections.heading: Use a final checklist before sharing the minutes

items: Review every item listed under decisions and locate supporting transcript wording.
Review every action item separately for task, owner, deadline, and dependency.
Remove deadlines or owners that were inferred rather than stated.
Move tentative proposals and unresolved questions out of the confirmed decisions section.
Preserve uncertainty when the transcript says something is possible or unconfirmed.
Check names, numbers, dates, and technical terms for transcription errors.
If an important point remains ambiguous, mark it for confirmation instead of rewriting it as certain.

blocks.text: The practical rule is to treat AI-generated minutes as a structured draft, not as an authoritative record. The more consequential the decision or commitment, the more important it is to trace the wording back to the transcript and, where necessary, confirm it with the meeting participants.

verification.env: ChatGPT Python tool · Python 3.x · standard library pathlib, sys
items: The first run completed successfully and created outputs/minutes_check_report.txt.
All five checks returned PASS: revised-template decision, Leo's October 6 action, Sara's review action, unresolved appendix decision, and uncertain October 8 supplier-data date.
The generated report contained exactly the five PASS lines followed by the four stated manual-review reminders.
The transcript remained byte-for-byte unchanged after execution.
A second run stopped with the stated message because outputs already existed, so the prior report was not overwritten.

The article's interpretation is consistent with the transcript: Sara has no calendar deadline, October 8 applies only to possible supplier-data arrival, the appendix remains unresolved, and the supplier date remains explicitly unconfirmed.
limits: Exact phrase matching cannot validate paraphrases or broader transcript context.
The Python environment emitted an unrelated spreadsheet-runtime warmup warning on stderr; it did not affect the article script or its verified output.
